Climate-informed public-health surveillance also requires compatible geospatial/temporal units, joint indicators, uncertainty handling, thresholds, cross-sector governance and explicit action protocols. public.text: The climate-related requirement is limited to ingesting sensor or data streams. Climate-informed public-health surveillance also requires compatible geospatial/temporal units, joint indicators, uncertainty handling, thresholds, cross-sector governance and explicit action protocols. Data integration without a decision pathway may produce dashboards without preparedness.
public.suggestedRevision:
Expand the requirement to include governed climate–health indicator definitions, geospatial/temporal alignment, provenance and forecast uncertainty, alert thresholds, cross-sector data-sharing agreements, responsible decision owners, response protocols and evaluation of false positives/negatives and unequal impacts. In other words, these integrations have functional requirements as well as governance models. 

In more technical detail: we should also address the temporal and spatial resolution mismatch between climate data (often gridded, continuous, sub-daily) and routine health surveillance data (facility-based, weekly/monthly, point-located), since this reconciliation — not just data receipt — is the actual technical challenge climate-health integration efforts like DHIS2's Chap Modeling Platform have had to solve. Distinguish between passively receiving environmental data streams for monitoring/analysis and the more demanding case of climate-driven predictive/forecasting models (e.g., climate-sensitive disease forecasting), since the latter requires defining model outputs and decision-support integration as a distinct capability rather than framed around communicable disease surveillance.
